title: Volcanoes and the Ring of Fire
objective: After this level you can explain why volcanoes form where they do and locate the Ring of Fire.
summary: Magma rises because it's lighter than solid rock. Most volcanoes sit near plate boundaries, especially the Ring of Fire around the Pacific; Hawaii's sit over a hotspot instead.

cards.headline: Trace the rim of the Pacific and you've found most of the world's volcanoes.
cards.body: About 75% of them sit in one long loop. Where volcanoes grow isn't random. It's a map of the plates.

cards.headline: Why melted rock comes up
cards.body: Deep underground, some rock melts into magma. Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it rises. Where it breaks through the surface, you get a volcano, and the magma gets a new name: lava. The vast majority of eruptions happen near Level 12's plate boundaries.

cards.headline: The Ring of Fire
cards.body: Around much of the Pacific, plates meet and one dives beneath another. The sinking rock melts into magma that feeds volcanoes, strung along plate boundaries about 40,000 km long: the Ring of Fire. It holds about 75% of Earth's volcanoes, more than 450, and about 90% of its earthquakes. The Pacific, Level 8's biggest ocean, also has the busiest rim.
cards.callout: About 75% of volcanoes · about 90% of earthquakes

cards.fact: Hawaii's volcanoes are nowhere near a plate boundary.
cards.context: They sit mid-plate, more than 3,200 km from the nearest edge, over a hotspot: a stationary source of heat deep in the mantle. The Pacific Plate slides over it like paper over a candle. Each island gets carried off the hotspot in turn and its volcanoes die out. That's why the Big Island, still over it, is the youngest.

cards.headline: Volcanoes: located
learned: Magma rises because it's lighter than solid rock
Most eruptions happen near plate boundaries
The Ring of Fire holds about 75% of volcanoes
Hawaii grew over a hotspot, far from any boundary

questions.prompt: About what share of Earth's volcanoes lie along the Ring of Fire?

options.label: About 10%
options.rationale: Far too few: most volcanoes are there.

options.label: About 25%
options.rationale: It's the majority, not a quarter.

questions.explanation: About 75% of Earth's volcanoes, more than 450, line the Ring of Fire, along with about 90% of its earthquakes.

questions.prompt: Why do the Hawaiian islands get older the farther they are from the Big Island?

options.label: The plate carries each island off a fixed hotspot
The hotspot itself is drifting east
options.rationale: The hotspot stays put; the plate moves.

options.label: Older islands sank and rose again
options.rationale: They were carried away, not sunk and raised.

options.label: Erosion makes islands look older
options.rationale: They really are older: they formed earlier.

questions.explanation: The Pacific Plate slides over a stationary hotspot. Each island forms over it, then gets carried away and goes quiet.

questions.prompt: From Level 12: along the Ring of Fire, one plate dives beneath another. Why does that make volcanoes?

options.label: The plates rub and heat the air above
options.rationale: The heat comes from rock melting underground.

options.label: The sinking rock melts into magma that rises
New crust forms as the plates pull apart
Ocean water boils through the crust
options.rationale: The fuel is melted rock, not water.

questions.explanation: At a convergent boundary the sinking plate's rock melts. The magma is lighter than solid rock, so it rises and erupts.
